lessons.title: Electric fields and potential
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — electric fields and capacitors (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Use Coulomb's law and define electric field strength E = F/q and electric potential V
Use E = V/d for a uniform field and the potential V = Q/(4πε₀r) of a point charge
Analyse the motion of a charged particle accelerated or deflected in an electric field
reviewNotes: Constants used: e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s; mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg; ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m; μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m.
Whether the syllabus requires gravitational–electric analogies and E = −dV/dx is unclear.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Field and potential
blocks.md:
**Coulomb's law**: F = Q₁Q₂/(4πε₀r²) for two point charges (1/4πε₀ = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻² using ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹); like charges repel, unlike attract.

**Electric field strength** E = F/q (N C⁻¹ = V m⁻¹), the force per unit positive charge; for a point charge **E = Q/(4πε₀r²)**. **Potential** V = work per unit positive charge brought from infinity: **V = Q/(4πε₀r)** (J C⁻¹ = V).

blocks.title: Uniform field and moving charges
blocks.md:
Between parallel plates separated by d with pd V: **E = V/d** (uniform). A charge q accelerated through a pd V gains kinetic energy **½mv² = qV**.

In the field the force is F = qE and a = qE/m: a charge entering at right angles to the field follows a **parabola** (like a projectile: constant velocity along the plates, constant acceleration across them).

blocks.caption: Uniform field between parallel plates; an electron entering horizontally follows a parabola towards the positive plate.
blocks.alt: Two horizontal charged plates with vertical field lines and a red curved path of an electron bending toward the positive plate.

blocks.title: Field lines and equipotentials
blocks.md: Field lines show the direction of the force on a positive charge: from + to −, closer together where the field is stronger, and they cross equipotentials at right angles. Field strength is minus the potential gradient: **E = −dV/dx**. No work is done moving a charge along an equipotential.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Treating E as a scalar: it is a vector (add fields from several charges as vectors); V is a scalar (add with signs).
- Using r as the distance in cm: use metres.
- Forgetting that the force on an electron is opposite to the field direction.
- Gravity is usually negligible for electrons and ions: do not include it.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Electron gun
blocks.statement: An electron is accelerated from rest through a pd of 2.0 kV. Find its final speed (e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg).
steps: v = √(2eV/m) = √(2 × 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ ÷ 9.11 × 10⁻³¹) = 2.65 × 10⁷ m/s (about 9 % of c: relativistic effects are small).

blocks.title: Example 2 — Point charge and plates
blocks.statement: (a) Find E and V at 0.10 m from a point charge of 2.0 nC. (b) Find E between plates 4.0 cm apart with 800 V across them, and the force on an electron there.
steps: F = eE = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2.0 × 10⁴ = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ N (weight of the electron is only 9 × 10⁻³⁰ N).

lessons.title: Capacitors and the RC circuit
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — electric fields and capacitors (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Define capacitance and use C = Q/V, the parallel-plate formula and the energy stored W = ½CV²
Combine capacitors in series and parallel
Analyse the charging and discharging of a capacitor through a resistor using the time constant RC
reviewNotes: Constants used: e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s; mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg; ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m; μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m.
The charging formula and half-time t½ = 0.693RC are stated without proof; whether the board requires the derivation by integration is unknown.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Capacitance and energy
blocks.md:
A **capacitor** stores charge. **Capacitance C = Q/V** (farad, F = C V⁻¹). For two parallel plates of area A separated by d in air: **C = ε₀A/d** (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F m⁻¹); a dielectric of relative permittivity ε_r multiplies C by ε_r.

The energy stored is the area under the V–Q graph: **W = ½QV = ½CV² = Q²/2C**.

blocks.title: Combinations and the RC circuit
blocks.md:
Parallel: **C = C₁ + C₂ + …** (same V). Series: **1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + …** (same Q).

Discharge through a resistor R: **Q = Q₀e^(−t/RC)**, and V and I decay in the same way. The **time constant τ = RC** (seconds) is the time for Q to fall to 1/e ≈ 37 % of Q₀. Time to fall to half: t½ = 0.693 RC. Charging: Q = Q₀(1 − e^(−t/RC)).

blocks.caption: Discharge of a capacitor: V = V₀e^(−t/RC) with τ = RC = 4.7 s; at t = τ the pd has fallen to 1/e of its initial value.
blocks.alt: An exponentially decaying curve starting at 9 volts and falling to about 3.3 volts at 4.7 seconds.

blocks.title: Method for RC problems
blocks.md:
1. Compute τ = RC with R in ohms and C in farads (μF = 10⁻⁶ F).
2. Use V = V₀e^(−t/τ) for discharge; to find a time, take natural logs: t = τ ln(V₀/V).
3. A graph of ln V against t is a straight line with gradient −1/RC.
4. The initial current is I₀ = V₀/R.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Forgetting the units: μF must be converted to farads before multiplying by ohms.
- Using the series formula for parallel capacitors (and vice versa).
- Saying current flows through the dielectric: charge flows round the circuit and the plates charge up.
- Using a calculator in degree mode with exponentials (not needed) or confusing ln and log.
